To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a new class of monodentates, bearing an internal guanidinium group, has been designed and that these ligands have been shown to stabilize transition states by secondary ligand-substrate interactions, leading to highly efficient catalysis.

(i) a secondary substrate-ligation interaction can be a powerful tool to achieve selectivity in homogeneous catalysis, (ii) this interaction can be exploited in a library of monodendate phosphane ligand, (iii) this interaction is a key feature in the design of catalysts for regiospecific hydroformylation of unsaturated carboxyilc acids and other carboxylate-containing substrates.
the guanidine receptor ligands are highly efficient in promoting the regioselective rhodium-catalyzed hydroformylation of unsaturated carboxy acids.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a new class of ligands, the guanidinyl phosphane ligands (GAP ligands).
the design of new catalysts for the selective hydroformylation of functionalized alkenes and the mechanistic study of the catalytic process.

the design and synthesis of new ligand classes and their application to transition-metal catalysis, with a particular emphasis on the development of novel catalytic systems for regioselectivity control in hydroformylation and other C-C and C-X bond-forming reactions.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified an entirely new design principle for catalysts, which is based on a supramolecular ligand-substrate interaction in the transition state.
the supramolecular interaction between a transition metal catalyst and a substrate can be exploited to design a new class of transition-metal catalysts for highly efficient catalysis.
a new design principle of transition-state stabilization has been established.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the secondary ligand-substrate interaction is an efficient and general strategy for transition metal catalysis.

the design and application of supramolecular ligands for catalysis is not restricted to the well-known hydrogen bond donors and acceptors but can also be extended to other types of noncovalent interactions.
transition-state stabilization by secondary substrate-ligands is a new design principle that can be used for the rational design of highly efficient catalysts.
